guide.physics.debug.p2: Fitted wireframes for Compound / Mesh Colliders are density-controlled by distance: at most 10 objects within 22 meters of the camera draw the full mesh, the rest fall back to bounds boxes; a single triangle mesh overlay is capped at 800 lines to protect the debug-line buffer.
guide.physics.debug.t1: When chasing contact issues, pause first and then step frame by frame with the Contacts switch on — watching contact points and normals is the most direct way.
guide.physics.debug.title: Collider Visualization & Physics Debugger
guide.physics.layers.p1: The engine provides 32 fixed physics layers (Unity-compatible). Layer names come from the Tags & Layers configuration in Project Settings; the Layer Collision Matrix is edited on the Physics page — checks are symmetric, and unchecking a cell makes the two layers ignore each other.
guide.physics.layers.p2: The Layer Collision Matrix panel entry is a redirect shim: opening it automatically focuses the Physics page of Project Settings.
guide.physics.layers.p3: Wiring status: when entering Play, the editor pushes the matrix and layer names into the engine, and each body derives a (group, mask) pair from its layer for Bullet filtering; raycasts and shape queries are filtered by layer mask as well.
guide.physics.layers.s1: On the Physics page, expand the Layer Collision Matrix and uncheck the cell where two layers intersect.
guide.physics.layers.s2: Assign those two layers to two entities via the Layer dropdown on their Rigidbody components.
guide.physics.layers.s3: Enter Play: the two entities pass through each other while collisions with other layers are unaffected.
guide.physics.layers.t1: The Physics Debugger panel edits the same matrix, which is handy while debugging; changes from either place persist immediately.
guide.physics.layers.title: Physics Layers & Collision Filtering
guide.physics.layers.w1: The 2D layer matrix currently has no runtime consumer — Box2D bodies are not assigned layers yet, so collision filtering only applies to 3D.
guide.physics.overview.b1: The fixed timestep comes from Fixed Timestep on the Time page; physics catches up on a fixed cadence, with a per-frame catch-up cap to avoid a death spiral after a stall.
guide.physics.overview.b2: Gravity defaults to (0, -9.81, 0) and affects every rigid body with Use Gravity checked. Uncheck Use Gravity to exempt a body; Gravity Scale tunes it per body (0 is treated as uninitialized and behaves as 1.0).
guide.physics.overview.p1: JCE physics consists of two worlds: a Bullet-based 3D rigid-body world and an independent Box2D 2D world. Both are stepped by the runtime at a fixed timestep only in Play mode; while editing, the scene is not simulated.
guide.physics.overview.p2: Project-level physics parameters live in Project Settings under the Physics / Physics 2D pages: gravity, solver iteration counts, contact offset, bounce and sleep thresholds, query switches, and the Layer Collision Matrix. Changes persist with the project settings and are read the next time you enter Play.
guide.physics.overview.t1: Project settings are read once when the Play session is created — after editing, stop and re-enter Play for changes to take effect.
guide.physics.overview.title: Physics Overview & Project Settings
guide.physics.overview.w1: A Play session currently consumes only the Y component of gravity from the Physics page plus the fixed timestep from the Time page; solver iterations, contact offset, bounce/sleep thresholds and query switches are editable and saved, but not yet wired into the Play runtime.
guide.physics.overview.w2: The separate gravity on the Physics 2D page is likewise not wired yet: the 2D world currently shares the same Y gravity as the 3D world.
guide.physics.physics2d.b1: Rigidbody 2D: body type (static / kinematic / dynamic), mass, friction, restitution, fixed rotation; a dynamic body with mass 0 is treated as static.
guide.physics.physics2d.b2: Collider 2D: five shapes — box / circle / capsule / edge / polygon — plus offset, friction and restitution; without a Collider 2D, a placeholder unit box is created from the XY scale. The Scene view draws 2D outlines per shape.
guide.physics.physics2d.b3: When the observer enters or exits a region, ENTER / EXIT logs are emitted (visible in the Console); SavePoint regions automatically write a save snapshot on enter. The Scene view gizmo matches the runtime test exactly.
guide.physics.physics2d.p1: 2D physics is an independent Box2D world simulated in the XY plane: at spawn it takes the Transform's X/Y position and Z rotation, and dynamic bodies write position and angle back to the entity every fixed step.
guide.physics.physics2d.p2: Tilemap Collider 2D requires a Tilemap component on the same entity: in Play, the solid cells of the .tilemap.json are greedily merged into a few rectangles attached to a single static body; its own trigger, friction and restitution fields are consumed.
guide.physics.physics2d.p3: A Trigger Volume is a 3D gameplay region, not a physics collider: its shape is AABB / sphere / OBB, the center is an offset from the entity's world position, and half extents are interpreted in world units (not multiplied by scale). The runtime tracks a single observer — the scene's Character Controller if present, otherwise the camera.
guide.physics.physics2d.s1: Add a Trigger Volume to an entity, pick a shape and adjust the center and half extents (the gizmo previews live).
guide.physics.physics2d.s2: Enter Play and walk the character into the region.
guide.physics.physics2d.s3: Confirm the trigger ENTER / EXIT logs in the Console.
guide.physics.physics2d.t1: Tilemaps are painted in the Tile Palette panel; the Tilemap component's inspector has an 'Edit in Tile Palette' shortcut button.
guide.physics.physics2d.title: 2D Physics, Tilemaps & Triggers
guide.physics.physics2d.w1: Runtime shape limits: Edge is approximated as a single horizontal segment of length size.x; Polygon degrades to its bounding box; the Collider 2D 'Is Trigger' flag does not yet create a Box2D sensor.
guide.physics.physics2d.w2: Even if the tilemap entity also carries a dynamic Rigidbody 2D, the tilemap collider stays static (with a log warning); moving tilemap colliders are not supported yet.
guide.physics.physics2d.w3: The Fire Stay Events and Tag fields are saved with the scene but not consumed by the runtime yet — only ENTER / EXIT take effect.
guide.physics.title: Physics
guide.play.console.b1: Click to select a line, Ctrl-click to toggle, Shift-click for a range; Ctrl+C or the context menu's 'Copy' copies the selection, 'Copy All' copies every line visible under the current filter.
guide.play.console.b2: When a message contains a path:line reference, hovering shows a hint and double-clicking the row opens the file in the File Viewer.
guide.play.console.b3: The command line at the bottom supports clear, help, echo <msg>, plus play / stop / pause to control the Play session directly.
guide.play.console.p1: The Console shows logs from the editor and the Play session. The toolbar offers: a Clear button, four level toggles (Log / Warning / Error / Debug — Debug is off by default), Collapse (merges consecutive identical lines of the same level into one with an xN counter), Clear-on-Play (clears automatically each time Play starts) and Auto-scroll; the search box below filters by case-insensitive substring.
guide.play.console.tip1: When debugging Play issues, enable Clear-on-Play so each run shows only that session's output.
guide.play.console.title: Console: Log Filtering & Commands
guide.play.gameview.b1: Click the viewport to capture the mouse and enter the FPS fly camera: WASD to move, Space up, Shift down, Ctrl for 5x speed.
guide.play.gameview.b2: Hold Alt to temporarily release the cursor, press ESC to fully exit capture; stopping Play also releases it.
guide.play.gameview.b3: During Play, if the scene has a CharacterController, captured move / jump / sprint input drives the character directly (using the Input Manager action bindings); press V to switch between first- and third-person follow cameras. The third-person boom collides with the scene and shortens automatically so it never clips through walls.
guide.play.gameview.p1: The Game view is the runtime viewport. Toolbar, left to right: aspect ratio (Free / 16:9 / 16:10 / 4:3 / 21:9 / 1:1 — non-Free letterboxes and centers the image), renderer backend selector, a stats toggle (bottom-left overlay with backend, frame rate and render resolution), and the run-mode switch.
guide.play.gameview.p2: There are two run modes: Editor Simulation runs the scene embedded in the viewport, with a dropdown next to it to pick the game module; External Game launches the configured game executable with > (pick the exe with the ... button) and stops it with []; the process's standard output is forwarded to the Console with a [run] prefix.
guide.play.gameview.tip1: If an active virtual camera (VCam) exists in the scene, it takes over the Game view camera during Play, with priority over player-follow and free-fly.
guide.play.gameview.title: Game View
guide.play.gameview.warn1: Picking a renderer backend only writes the editor config — bgfx cannot hot-swap backends, so the editor must be restarted for it to apply; while the choice differs from the live backend, the toolbar shows a hint.
guide.play.input.b1: Play (Editor Simulation) reads the panel's live state directly: keyboard binding changes apply instantly, even without saving.
guide.play.input.p1: The Input Manager organizes input as actions plus bindings: each action has a unique name and a set of bindings of type key / mouse button / gamepad button / gamepad axis, with scale and deadzone. Keyboard binding codes are SDL scancodes. The whole table is saved to .jce/input_actions.json in your user directory.
guide.play.input.p2: On first use the panel is seeded from the engine's canonical FPS defaults: WASD to move, Space = jump, Left Shift = sprint; on gamepad, left stick to move, right stick to look, South (A) = jump, L3 = sprint.
guide.play.input.s1: Click 'Add Action' to create an action and rename it on the right (e.g. interact).
guide.play.input.s2: Click '+ Binding' to add a binding, choose the type and enter the code, adjusting scale and deadzone as needed.
guide.play.input.s3: Click 'Save' to write input_actions.json; 'Reset Defaults' returns to the engine default table, 'Reload' discards in-memory changes and re-reads the file.
guide.play.input.tip1: Gamepad bindings are evaluated during editor Play — a pad drives the character as soon as you move it, with no need to click the viewport first. Mouse bindings are still consumed only in the shipped game by the engine runtime.
guide.play.input.tip2: A shipped game first reads .jce/input_actions.json next to its working directory (shipped with the game), then falls back to the per-user file, and finally to the engine's default FPS table.
guide.play.input.title: Input System: Actions & Bindings
guide.play.l10n.b1: The preview-locale dropdown drives the editor's live localization table: UIText in the Game view and the Play session switches language instantly; saving the tables also hot-refreshes the current locale.
guide.play.l10n.p1: Game string tables live in i18n/<locale>.json under the project's source assets. With a project open, the Localization page of Project Settings provides a key-by-locale grid editor and shows the editor UI language (read-only) for contrast — the two are completely separate systems.
guide.play.l10n.s1: Open Project Settings (File menu, or Ctrl+Shift+P) and switch to the Localization page.
guide.play.l10n.s2: Type a key name (e.g. ui.title) into the key box and click 'Add Key'; type a lowercase locale code (e.g. zh_cn) into the locale box and click 'Add Locale' — saving creates i18n/<code>.json.
guide.play.l10n.s3: Fill in the text per locale in the grid and click 'Save': saving writes the union of keys to every locale file (missing values as empty strings), so locale files never drift out of key parity.
guide.play.l10n.s4: On an entity's UIText component, set the locale key: next to the input there is a picker over the string tables and a live preview resolved in the current preview locale; at runtime the key's translation overrides the Text field.
guide.play.l10n.tip1: A shipped game reads i18n/<locale>.json from the mounted PAK and picks the operating system's preferred language at startup, falling back to en; the host can also specify the locale explicitly.
guide.play.l10n.title: Game Localization (String Tables)
guide.play.l10n.warn1: Keys marked [L] are protected keys consumed by the engine's built-in pause / settings menu — you can edit their translations but cannot delete them.
guide.play.playmode.hk3: Step one frame (1/60 s) while paused
guide.play.playmode.p1: Run the current scene right inside the editor: the > / || / [] buttons at the top-right of the menu bar control the Play session. Once Play starts, the engine runtime takes over the scene — physics simulates, animation state machines activate, AudioSources start playing, and character controllers can be driven from the Game view.
guide.play.playmode.p2: The Play session is governed by Project Settings: the Time page's fixed timestep, the Physics page's gravity and layer collision matrix, and the Audio page's master volume and Doppler factor all take effect the moment Play starts.
guide.play.playmode.s1: Click the > button at the top-right of the menu bar (or use the hotkey above) to enter Play; the button turns into || and highlights green.
guide.play.playmode.s2: While running, click || to pause and click it again to resume; while paused, use the step hotkey to advance frame by frame and inspect physics and animation details.
guide.play.playmode.s3: Click [] to stop — the scene rolls back to the state it had before Play, and you can keep editing.
guide.play.playmode.tip1: The Game view toolbar carries the same > / || / [] buttons, plus an extra >| step button while paused.
guide.play.playmode.title: Play Mode: Run, Pause, Step
guide.play.playmode.warn1: Entering Play captures a snapshot of the whole scene, and stopping restores it unconditionally: every change made during Play (transforms, components, new entities) is lost on stop. To keep a change, stop Play first, then edit.
guide.play.playmode.warn2: Creating / opening / loading a scene during Play automatically stops Play first, then switches scenes.
guide.play.saves.p1: The Save Browser recursively scans the project's saves directory and lists every .jsnp snapshot file with its size, format version, section count and header validity.
guide.play.saves.p2: Runtime save points (SavePoint) from Play sessions are written to the same <project>/saves directory, so saves produced while the game runs can be inspected and replayed here.
guide.play.saves.s1: Click 'Refresh' to rescan the saves directory.
guide.play.saves.s2: Click 'Load' on a row: the current edit scene is rebuilt from the snapshot's scene / ECS section, and the result is shown below the table.
guide.play.saves.tip1: The whole load is wrapped into a single undoable step: Ctrl+Z brings back the scene as it was before the load.
guide.play.saves.title: Save Browser
guide.play.saves.warn1: Loading a snapshot stops Play first and replaces the entire current scene — make sure you do not need the current edit state before loading.
guide.play.title: Run & Debug
guide.render.camera.p1: The Camera component defines framing for the Game view and Play mode. Fields: field of view, near/far clip planes, orthographic toggle, primary-camera flag, stack index, and clear mode (Skybox/Color/Depth Only/Nothing).
guide.render.camera.p2: The Virtual Camera component provides the camera-direction system: name, priority, active toggle, track mode (None/Follow/Look At/Follow + Look At), FOV, damping, and static position/look-at/follow-offset values; follow and look-at targets take entity IDs, where 0 means no target and falls back to the static values.
guide.render.camera.p3: The Virtual Camera Manager lists every vcam sorted by priority descending, with inline editing of name, priority, active flag and FOV; a green star marks the currently live camera, and Ping selects the owning entity.
guide.render.camera.s1: Add a Virtual Camera component to an entity, pick a track mode and fill in the target entity IDs.
guide.render.camera.s2: Use priority to decide which vcam wins: the highest-priority active one takes over; the Solo button temporarily raises priority to 9999 for instant auditioning.
guide.render.camera.s3: Enter Play mode to verify: in Play mode the virtual camera takes over the Game view camera, and damping smooths transitions.
guide.render.camera.tip1: In edit mode the Scene view still uses the editor camera; check virtual-camera results in the Game view and in Play mode.
guide.render.camera.title: Cameras & Virtual Cameras
guide.render.lights.hk2: Frame the selected light in the viewport to check its direction and shadows
guide.render.lights.p1: Lights are Light components attached to entities, in three types — directional, point, and spot. You can convert between types at any time via the Type dropdown in the Inspector; color and intensity are preserved where possible.
guide.render.lights.p2: Spot lights support cookie textures and IES photometric profiles; directional lights support a world-aligned directional cookie (an orthographic projection centred on the camera).
guide.render.lights.p3: Shadow filter quality is tiered by the project quality presets (1-tap/3x3/5x5) and listed — together with shadow resolution and max lights — in the four-tier comparison matrix on the Project Settings Quality page, with one-click apply.
guide.render.lights.s1: Create a directional or point light via the GameObject → Light menu; the new entity is selected automatically.
guide.render.lights.s2: Set the light color and intensity in the Inspector.
guide.render.lights.s3: Aim directional and spot lights with Azimuth/Elevation or the rotation dial below: drag the sun handle — the center means shining straight down, the edge means horizontal.
guide.render.lights.s4: Set the radius for point and spot lights; for spot lights also tune the inner/outer cone angles to control the edge softness.
guide.render.lights.s5: Enable "Casts Shadow"; for spot and point lights you can also fine-tune the shadow bias to remove self-shadowing artifacts.
guide.render.lights.tip1: To overview or batch-edit every light in the scene, the Light Explorer inner tab under the Lighting Settings tab is the fastest tool.
guide.render.lights.title: Light Components: Directional, Point, Spot
guide.render.lights.warn1: In the current version the directional cookie shares one sampler with spot cookies: when both exist, the first eligible spot cookie wins.
guide.render.lights.warn2: Cascaded shadows (CSM) are driven only by the scene's first directional light; point and spot lights use local shadow maps, and point-light shadows cover only the downward hemisphere.
guide.render.matgraph.insp.p1: The Shader Inspector tab compiles a .sc for any backend and shows three things the source alone cannot answer: what the preprocessor actually produced, which uniforms and attributes survived into the blob, and the compiled code itself.
guide.render.matgraph.insp.s1: Point the source field at a .sc, or press Use generated to take the one the Material Graph last wrote.
guide.render.matgraph.insp.s2: Choose a target backend. It does not have to be the one the editor is running on -- that is how you find out whether a shader compiles on Metal from a Windows machine.
guide.render.matgraph.insp.s3: Read the Reflection tab first: a uniform missing there never reached the GPU, whatever the source says.
guide.render.matgraph.insp.warn1: Instruction counts come from the D3D disassembly, so they appear for DirectX targets only. On other backends the count is reported as unavailable rather than as zero.
guide.render.matgraph.p1: The Material Graph is the node-based material and shader authoring panel, and also hosts the graph-authoring workbench: Shader Graph, VFX Graph and Particle Editor sit under it as sibling tabs; the Shader Graph tab is an explainer page — actual node editing happens in the Material Graph.
guide.render.matgraph.p2: Toolbar, left to right: graph file path (.matgraph.json), Save Graph, Load Graph, Compile -> .mat.json, Generate Shader (.sc), Compile & Bind, Import .mat.json. The left side of the panel holds the preview sphere and compile log, the right side the node canvas.
guide.render.matgraph.p3: The "Open Graph" button next to the material field jumps from the Mesh Renderer back into the Material Graph (deriving a graph from the .mat.json when none exists); with multiple entities selected, "Assign to Selection" applies the current material to every selected Mesh Renderer.
guide.render.matgraph.p4: If you edit shader source on disk directly, use Edit → Reload Shaders to hot-reload without restarting the editor.
guide.render.matgraph.s1: Set the graph file path first and click Save Graph: the output paths for compiling and shader generation are derived from it.
guide.render.matgraph.s2: Build nodes on the canvas and wire them into the PBR Output's BaseColor, Metallic, Roughness and Emissive sockets.
guide.render.matgraph.s3: Click "Compile -> .mat.json": the graph is evaluated into PBR material parameters and texture paths and written to the .mat.json; the log lists each evaluated slot.
guide.render.matgraph.s4: Put the generated .mat.json into the Mesh Renderer component's Materials field (or drag it in from the Asset Browser) — the entity applies the new material immediately.
guide.render.matgraph.s5: Advanced: "Generate Shader (.sc)" exports the graph as BGFX fragment shader source; "Compile & Bind" compiles it in the background and binds the program to the preview sphere.
guide.render.matgraph.tip1: Shader compilation runs asynchronously on a worker thread; while it runs, the Compile & Bind button is greyed out and shows compiling… without blocking the editor.
guide.render.matgraph.title: Material Graph & Shader Graph
guide.render.matgraph.warn1: Compilation requires a PBR Output node on the canvas and a non-empty file path; otherwise errors are reported in the log and the Console.
guide.render.pipeline.b1: Presets: Low/Mid/High/Ultra, applied with one click.
guide.render.pipeline.b2: Feature switches: CSM shadows, SSAO, SSR, TAA, bloom, volumetric fog, GPU particles (requires compute shaders, greyed out on unsupported devices), motion blur, cloth simulation.
guide.render.pipeline.b3: Quality: shadow resolution 512-4096, texture LOD bias 0-3, cascade count 1-4, MSAA (Off/2x/4x/8x), render scale 0.25-2.0, post-processing quality.
guide.render.pipeline.b4: Format: HDR color buffer and depth pre-pass.
guide.render.pipeline.p1: The Render Pipeline tab organizes the whole pipeline's features and quality into a savable/loadable .rp.json asset, with Save and Load buttons at the top; every change is applied to the running renderer immediately.
guide.render.pipeline.p2: The Project Settings Quality page shows the same pipeline as a Low/Mid/High/Ultra comparison matrix, including the shadow filter tiers (1-tap/3x3/5x5) and max lights, with one-click apply to the current session.
guide.render.pipeline.p3: The Frame Debugger is a tab of the Profiling workbench and offers three layers of real data: bgfx frame totals (draw/compute/blit counts, CPU/GPU milliseconds, resources and GPU memory), the per-view GPU/CPU table, and render-queue stats: commands to submits, merged instance batches, total instances, and per-level LOD pick counts.
guide.render.pipeline.p4: To watch LOD switching directly: the Debug menu's "Toggle Demo LOD" attaches a demo LOD chain (cube 8 m / sphere 18 m / plane 35 m) on the scene renderer; combine the Frame Debugger's LOD counters with the Scene view to observe distance switching.
guide.render.pipeline.tip1: The texture LOD bias is a live global mip-bias control, not an .rp.json field; the low-memory pressure bridge may overwrite a manual value when memory pressure changes.
guide.render.pipeline.title: Render Pipeline & Performance
guide.render.pipeline.warn1: When the Frame Debugger shows "render queue not used this frame", the batching path is disabled and the batching/instancing numbers are unavailable.
guide.render.postfx.b4: Vignette (intensity/smoothness), chromatic aberration (strength), and a grayscale toggle.
guide.render.postfx.p1: Post-processing is edited on the Post-Processing tab of the Rendering workbench. Parameters are written into the current scene's rendering settings, saved with the scene, and previewed live in the editor viewport.
guide.render.postfx.p2: The Custom Pass is a style-agnostic generic post effect: enter a shader name, whether it needs depth, and up to 8 vec4 parameter rows; the Look dropdown ships nine pre-tuned one-click looks — moebius, toon, painterly, lowpoly, pixel, psx, watercolor, comic, blueprint.
guide.render.postfx.p3: Mind the layering: the toggles on this tab are scene data, while Bloom/TAA and friends on the Render Pipeline tab are pipeline-level feature switches that affect the whole renderer.
guide.render.postfx.s1: Tick an effect's Enable checkbox and drag its parameters while watching the viewport live.
guide.render.postfx.s2: For a full stylized look, expand the Custom Pass and pick a look from the Look dropdown — it enables the pass and fills in the shader name and parameters automatically.
guide.render.postfx.s3: Use the screenshot hotkey to capture before/after frames for comparison.
guide.render.postfx.tip1: The custom shader name only commits when you press Enter, so the shader is not reloaded on every keystroke.
guide.render.postfx.title: Post-Processing
guide.render.postfx.warn1: "Reset All" restores this scene's post-processing parameters to defaults and clears the custom shader name, taking effect immediately — confirm before clicking.
guide.render.title: Rendering & Lighting
guide.render.workbench.b1: Environment: sky type (None/Procedural/HDRI), sky intensity, ambient intensity and color; it also embeds the editor for the scene's first Skybox component (HDR path, rotation, exposure, use-as-IBL toggle).
guide.render.workbench.b2: Directional Light: drives the scene's first directional light — color, intensity, yaw/pitch angles, and the shadow toggle.
guide.render.workbench.b3: Shadows (CSM): shadow distance, cascade count 1-4, split lambda, shadow-map resolution 512-4096, and soft-shadow mode (Off/PCF/VSM).
guide.render.workbench.b4: Image-Based Lighting (IBL): a read-only status area showing the Skybox HDR path currently driving IBL, plus the SH band and specular mip counts.
guide.render.workbench.b5: Fog: mode (None/Linear/Exp/Exp2) and color; linear mode uses start/end distances, exponential modes use density, plus volumetric-fog height falloff and height origin.
guide.render.workbench.h1: The five sections of the Settings tab
guide.render.workbench.h2: Time of day, weather, and the Light Explorer
guide.render.workbench.p1: Scene-level lighting and rendering settings live in the Rendering workbench, hosted by the Lighting Settings panel. The outer tabs across the top are: Lighting Settings, Post-Processing, Lightmap Bake, Reflection Probes, and Render Pipeline; later topics in this chapter cover each one.
guide.render.workbench.p2: Inside the Lighting Settings tab there are three inner tabs: Settings, Time of Day, and Light Explorer. The Window menu entries for Time of Day and Light Explorer jump straight to the matching inner tab.
guide.render.workbench.p3: The Time of Day inner tab's day-night and weather parameters serialize with the scene: enable toggle, hour (0-24), advance speed, latitude, dawn/dusk hours; weather supports clear/rain/snow with intensity. Below, the evaluated sun direction, color, fog and exposure are shown live.
guide.render.workbench.p4: The Light Explorer inner tab lists every light in the scene as a table, filterable by type, with inline editing of color, intensity, shadows and enabled state, plus a Ping button that selects the owning entity.
guide.render.workbench.p5: Ambient, fog, shadows and post-processing all belong to the current scene's rendering settings and are saved with the scene; remember to save the scene once you are happy.
guide.render.workbench.tip1: After changing the Skybox HDR path, the engine automatically re-convolves IBL on a worker thread and caches the result to disk: the first bake is slow, later reloads take milliseconds.
guide.render.workbench.tip2: When the advance speed is greater than 0, the hour slider is locked and advances automatically; to freeze a moment, set the speed to zero first, then drag the hour.
guide.render.workbench.title: The Lighting Workbench at a Glance
guide.render.workbench.warn1: The "Bake All Reflection Probes" button at the bottom of the Settings tab is currently a placeholder and does nothing. Use the Reflection Probes tab instead, or bake each probe from its component.
guide.scene.ai.p1: The AI Assistant describes what you want in words and gets a scene back. The answer is checked against the engine's own component schema before it can become a file, so a model cannot invent a field that would load as nothing.
guide.scene.ai.p2: The answer is written as a scene file, not applied over what you have open. Open it from the Asset Browser when you want to look at it — an assistant that replaced your work silently would be a worse assistant.
guide.scene.ai.s1: Set JCE_LLM_API_KEY in your environment before starting the editor. The editor never stores it.
guide.scene.ai.s2: Write the brief. A paragraph beats a sentence: say what the space is for, not only what is in it.
guide.scene.ai.s3: Leave 'Send for real' off the first time and press the button. You see the exact request, and nothing leaves the machine.
guide.scene.ai.s4: Turn it on and ask. Watch Tool output; the elapsed time and a Cancel button are there while it runs.
guide.scene.ai.s5: Name a Scene and turn on Verify to make the tool render the result and compare it with the before against a noise floor.
guide.scene.ai.tip1: The provider is a program, so a local model needs no key and no network at all: point Program at your runner and pass the brief file to it.
guide.scene.ai.title: Authoring with a language model
guide.scene.ai.warn1: A brief carries the shape of an unreleased game. 'Send for real' is what makes it leave this machine, and it is off again every time the panel is opened.
guide.scene.assetdrop.b1: Models (.fbx/.glb/.gltf/.obj/.dae and more): the default always creates a new entity. The drop lands on the real surface under the cursor (a scene raycast; empty space falls back to the ground plane) and is bottom-aligned by the mesh bounding box, so it never sinks halfway into the ground.
guide.scene.assetdrop.b2: Hold Alt and drop a model onto an existing mesh entity = replace its mesh and auto-extract the model's bundled material; without Alt an existing entity is never overwritten.
guide.scene.assetdrop.b3: Textures (.png/.jpg/.dds/.ktx2 and more) dropped onto a mesh entity are slotted automatically by filename: normal/nrm goes to normal, ao/occlusion to ambient occlusion, emissive to emissive, metallic/roughness to metallic-roughness, everything else to albedo.
guide.scene.assetdrop.b4: A .mat.json material file dropped onto a mesh entity = apply that material wholesale (texture references and all PBR parameters).
guide.scene.assetdrop.b5: HDR environment maps (.hdr/.exr) dropped anywhere in the viewport = set as the scene skybox; if the scene has no Skybox entity yet, one is created automatically.
guide.scene.assetdrop.p1: Drag files from the Asset Browser straight into the Scene viewport to populate the scene; the editor routes them by file type: models, textures, materials (.mat.json), and HDR environment maps each have dedicated behavior.
guide.scene.assetdrop.s1: Grab a model file in the Asset Browser and start dragging.
guide.scene.assetdrop.s2: Move into the Scene viewport: a semi-transparent placement preview (ghost) appears under the cursor; it uses the real mesh data, so the landing spot and alignment are what you see.
guide.scene.assetdrop.s3: Release the mouse to place: the new entity is named after the file (duplicates get _1, _2 suffixes), is selected immediately, and the Inspector syncs to it.
guide.scene.assetdrop.tip1: A glTF with a skeleton and animation clips automatically gets a Skeletal Animator component on drop and starts looping its first clip — the character moves the moment it lands.
guide.scene.assetdrop.title: Placing Assets by Drag and Drop
guide.scene.assetdrop.warn1: Dropping a texture on empty space does nothing; the Console explains it must be dropped onto a mesh entity. You also get a Console warning when the dragged file no longer exists on disk.
guide.scene.gizmo.b1: With a multi-selection the manipulator acts on the whole group: translation offsets everything; rotation/scale transform each entity's position and orientation around the manipulator location (combine with Center mode to rotate around the selection midpoint).
guide.scene.gizmo.b2: In 2D mode the manipulator is locked to the XY plane: Z translation, X/Y rotation, and Z scale are all locked.
guide.scene.gizmo.hk4: Toggle the manipulator between local and world space
guide.scene.gizmo.hk5: With a multi-selection, toggle the manipulator position: focused entity's pivot or the selection's geometric center
guide.scene.gizmo.p1: With an entity selected, the transform manipulator appears in the viewport. The T/R/S/D radio buttons on the left of the Scene toolbar map to translate/rotate/scale/pivot-edit; next to them sit the Local/World space toggle, the Snap settings popup, and the 2D/3D mode switch.
guide.scene.gizmo.p2: Hold Ctrl while dragging a handle to enable snapping; the step sizes are set per move/rotate/scale in the Scene toolbar's Snap popup, with reset defaults of 0.5, 15 degrees, and 0.25. Snapping still applies on the release frame, so the final value never drifts back to the unsnapped position.
guide.scene.gizmo.tip1: Press Esc mid-drag to cancel the operation immediately: the scene rolls back to the pre-drag state and no history entry is created.
guide.scene.gizmo.title: Transform Manipulator (Gizmo)
guide.scene.gizmo.warn1: Scale values are clamped to a minimum of 0.001 to prevent degenerate matrices. If you cannot see the manipulator, check the Gizmos switch under the viewport View menu's Show Flags, and the Show Gizmos option in Preferences.
guide.scene.hierarchy.b1: Click to select an entity; Ctrl+click adds to or removes from the selection; Shift+click range-selects from the last selected anchor; double-click focuses the scene camera on the entity.
guide.scene.hierarchy.b2: The dot button at the right of each row toggles the entity enabled/disabled: filled circle = enabled, hollow = disabled; disabled entities are drawn semi-transparent and are excluded from viewport picking and marquee selection.
guide.scene.hierarchy.b3: Drag an entity onto another row = make it a child; drag into the thin gap between rows (a blue insert line appears) = reorder among siblings; drag onto empty panel space = move back to the root. With a multi-selection the whole group moves together.
guide.scene.hierarchy.b4: With the panel focused, type a letter or digit to jump to and select the next entity whose name starts with that character; pressing the same key again within 1.5 seconds cycles through further matches.
guide.scene.hierarchy.hk1: Rename the focused entity (also available in the right-click menu)
guide.scene.hierarchy.hk2: Duplicate the selected entities (duplicates become the new selection)
guide.scene.hierarchy.hk3: Delete the selected entities (a confirmation dialog opens first)
guide.scene.hierarchy.p1: The Hierarchy panel lists every entity in the scene as a tree. The search box at the top filters by name, tag, or tag color (parent chains auto-expand when a child matches); the two combos below it are the tag-color filter and the sort mode (default order, by name, by tag).
guide.scene.hierarchy.p2: Right-click an entity for the context menu: Focus (F), Rename, Duplicate, Create Child (empty entity, 3D object, 2D object, camera, light), Prefab (Save As, Revert, Save As Variant), tag color and tag presets, Copy/Cut/Paste, Delete; right-clicking empty space shows a lean root-level menu (Create, Paste, Select All).
guide.scene.hierarchy.p3: The main menu offers the same creation entries, for example:
guide.scene.hierarchy.tip1: Cut entities show as semi-transparent 'ghost rows', so you can back out any time before pasting; Paste lands under the currently focused entity, or at the scene root when nothing is focused.
guide.scene.hierarchy.title: Hierarchy Panel: Organizing the Scene
guide.scene.pivot.p1: JCE uses a Maya-style pivot model: the entity's Transform position IS the pivot's world position, and the model is offset relative to the pivot. Press D (or Insert, or the D button on the Scene toolbar) to enter/leave pivot-edit mode.
guide.scene.pivot.p2: For exact values, open the Pivot section in the Inspector: enter the pivot's local position and orientation (Euler angles), read the world position (read-only), and use the two buttons Reset Pivot (zero it) and Center Pivot (move it to the model's bounding-box center).
guide.scene.pivot.s1: Select an entity and press D: a yellow crosshair marker appears in the viewport (the pivot position) along with a dim tether line to the model origin.
guide.scene.pivot.s2: Drag the pivot with the translate handles: the model does not move in the world at all; only the pivot position (and the Transform position readout) changes.
guide.scene.pivot.s3: Switch to the rotate handles to set the pivot orientation: this orientation becomes the entity's custom manipulation axes.
guide.scene.pivot.s4: Press D again to return to normal mode: with this entity single-selected, the translate/rotate handles now align to the axes you defined; scale is exempt and always operates on the entity's own axes.
guide.scene.pivot.tip1: Scale is disabled in pivot-edit mode (it auto-switches back to translate); pivots cannot be edited with a multi-selection — edit one entity's pivot at a time.
guide.scene.pivot.title: Pivot Editing (Maya-style)
guide.scene.pivot.warn1: Moving the pivot uses keep-the-model-still semantics: the Transform position number changes while the model's world position stays put. Seeing the number move is not a bug — the pivot was re-seated.
guide.scene.selection.b1: Hold the left button and drag to sweep a green marquee rectangle: on release, every entity the rectangle touches is selected; hold Ctrl or Shift to append to the existing selection.
guide.scene.selection.b2: Alt is reserved entirely for the camera: Alt+left orbits, Alt+middle pans, Alt+right dollies, and the wheel zooms. While Alt is held, no marquee starts and no context menu opens.
guide.scene.selection.b3: Each selected entity is marked with an orange diamond in the viewport; the focused entity also drives what the Inspector shows.
guide.scene.selection.hk1: Frame the selected entities (camera fits the selection bounds)
guide.scene.selection.hk2: Frame the whole scene (fit all entities)
guide.scene.selection.p1: Click in the Scene viewport to pick an entity: supported render backends use pixel-accurate GPU picking, otherwise it falls back to bounding-box ray casting. Ctrl or Shift+click adds/removes from the selection; clicking empty space clears it.
guide.scene.selection.p2: Right-clicking the viewport (without Alt) opens the scene menu: create entities, duplicate/delete the current selection, focus selected, switch the manipulator mode, and reset the camera or snap to top/front/side view presets.
guide.scene.selection.tip1: Disabled (hidden) entities are excluded from click picking and marquee selection; select them from the Hierarchy panel instead.
guide.scene.selection.title: Viewport Selection and Picking
guide.scene.title: Scene Editing
guide.scene.undo.b1: Manipulator drags are transactional: one full drag = one undo entry; pressing Esc mid-drag rolls back directly and leaves no entry.
guide.scene.undo.b2: Batch operations (multi-duplicate, bulk delete, multi-selection drags, and the like) also collapse into a single entry — one undo reverts the whole batch.
guide.scene.undo.b3: History depth: up to 30 snapshots with a total memory budget of 64 MB; when exceeded, the oldest entries are dropped automatically.
guide.scene.undo.p1: Almost every scene-editing operation is undoable: creating/deleting/duplicating entities, renames, reparenting, component and transform edits, viewport asset drops, and more. History is based on whole-scene snapshots, so restores are exact and reliable.
guide.scene.undo.p2: When you reach a good stopping point, save the scene:
guide.scene.undo.tip1: Any new edit clears the redo stack: after undoing, redo first if you still want that work back, then continue editing.
guide.scene.undo.title: Undo and Redo
guide.scene.undo.warn1: Undo/redo is disabled during Play mode (the runtime holds the scene). Play itself is a sandbox: stopping playback restores the scene state from before entering Play.
guide.start.first.p1: Follow these steps to build a runnable scene from scratch: one cube, one directional light, one camera.
guide.start.first.s1: Create a new scene (if the current scene has unsaved changes you will be asked first):
guide.start.first.s2: Right-click empty space in the Scene viewport and choose Create > 3D Object > Cube: the entity comes with a Mesh Renderer component, gets selected, and the Inspector is focused.
guide.start.first.s3: In the Inspector's Mesh Renderer section, the Shape dropdown swaps the built-in mesh to sphere/plane/capsule/cylinder.
guide.start.first.s4: Right-click the viewport again: Create > Light gives you a directional light, Create > Camera a game camera — the running game renders through it.
guide.start.first.s5: Save the scene (the first save opens a Save As dialog to pick the path):
guide.start.first.s6: Click ▶ at the top right of the menu bar (or press the play hotkey) to enter Play mode and watch the camera image in the Game panel; ■ stops and returns to editing.
guide.start.first.tip1: The main GameObject menu can create the same named entities, but those are empty entities with only a Transform — add components afterwards via the Inspector's Add Component button; its popup searches in any language and Enter adds the first match.
guide.start.first.title: Your First Scene (Hands-on)
guide.start.first.warn1: With unsaved changes the status bar marks the scene name with *; watch for the unsaved-changes confirmation before creating/opening scenes — discarding cannot be undone.
guide.start.howto.b1: The filter box at the top left narrows chapters and topics by title (matched in the current UI language).
guide.start.howto.b2: Hotkey chips show the binding that is actually in effect right now: they read the hotkey registry directly, so they update when you rebind keys; actions without a binding are marked as unbound.
guide.start.howto.b3: The Open buttons make the documented panel visible and focus its dock tab, so you can follow along with one click — for example, open the Console:
guide.start.howto.b4: Menu path rows list the real menu levels to click through, for example this guide's entry in the Help menu:
guide.start.howto.b5: Every article ends with Previous / Next topic buttons; the Hotkey Reference at the bottom of the chapter list is generated straight from the registry, so it never goes stale, and can be filtered by action, chord or id.

guide.start.howto.p2: You can reopen this guide at any time from the Help menu, or via the Window menu:
guide.start.howto.tip1: Want different keys? Rebind them on the hotkeys page under Edit > Preferences; this guide and menu hints show the new bindings immediately.
guide.start.howto.title: How to Use This Guide
guide.start.search.b1: Commands cover: scene and project file operations, build and packing, undo/redo, entity creation, view snapping and fullscreen/screenshot, layout presets, and visibility toggles for over twenty panels.
guide.start.search.b2: Matching runs against the localized label, the stable English id and the category name — whatever the UI language, typing in English or your own language both hit.
guide.start.search.p1: Can't remember which menu hides a feature? You have two weapons: the command palette and the global Search panel.
guide.start.search.p2: The command palette is a top-centered quick launcher: type to filter (VS Code-style subsequence fuzzy matching), use the up/down arrows to select, Enter to run, Esc to close.
guide.start.search.p3: The global Search panel offers three tabs, so one query searches three places:
guide.start.search.tab1: In Scene: substring match on entity names and tags; clicking a result selects that entity.
guide.start.search.tab2: Menus / Panels: cross-language search — a query in any installed language hits the same target (typing a Chinese term on an English UI still finds the panel); results carry a language tag, and clicking a panel result opens it directly.
guide.start.search.tab3: In Project: matches file paths plus the name/displayName fields inside .scene/.prefab/.material/.asset JSON files; clicking a result opens it in the File Viewer.
guide.start.search.title: Command Palette and Global Search
guide.start.search.warn1: The palette hotkey does not fire while a text field has focus or a modal dialog is open.
guide.start.title: Getting Started
guide.start.ui.debughelp: Debug: demo LOD toggle. Help: welcome screen, this official guide, about.
guide.start.ui.dock: Docking: drag a panel by its tab to rearrange — drop onto the middle of another panel to merge as tabs, onto an edge to split, or outside the main window to float it. If the layout gets messy:
guide.start.ui.edit: Edit: undo/redo, cut/copy/paste/duplicate, delete, preferences, and shader reload.
guide.start.ui.file: File: new/open/save/save-as for scenes, recent scenes and recent projects, new/open project, build settings and bundle packing, project settings, exit.
guide.start.ui.go: GameObject: create empty, 3D objects (cube/sphere/plane), camera, lights (directional/point). Note: this menu creates named entities with only a Transform — components are added later in the Inspector.
guide.start.ui.hkws: Switch to workspace 1 (see the Hotkey Reference chapter for the others):
guide.start.ui.p1: The main window has three parts: the menu bar on top (play controls at its right end), the dockable panel area in the middle, and the status bar at the bottom. Every panel can be rearranged by dragging.
guide.start.ui.play: Play controls sit at the far right of the menu bar: ▶ starts Play mode (it turns into ‖ pause while running), ■ stops and returns to edit mode.
guide.start.ui.preset: There are 10 layout presets (Default/Wide/Animation/2x2/Programmer/2D/Mobile Portrait/Cinematic/Profiling/Lighting); Reset Layout restores the default in one click.
guide.start.ui.status: Status bar (bottom of the window): FPS, current scene name (marked * with unsaved changes), selected entity count, play state, GPU tier (click to override for this session), and a ready indicator on the right.
guide.start.ui.title: UI Overview
guide.start.ui.warn1: While any modal dialog is open (New Project, Build Settings, ...) the entire menu bar is temporarily disabled — close the dialog first.
guide.start.ui.window: Window: visibility toggles for core panels and viewports, the eight workbenches, world tools, global search and this guide, plus layout presets and the status bar toggle.
guide.start.ui.ws: The middle of the menu bar also hosts a Maya-style workspace dropdown (Default/Modeling/Rigging/Animation/FX/Rendering/UV Editing and more); switching a workspace applies its layout and menu set.
guide.start.viewport.ctx: Right-click (without Alt) opens the context menu: create entities, duplicate/delete, focus selection, switch gizmo mode, reset the camera and top/front/side views.
guide.start.viewport.cube: The viewport corners host an axis indicator and a view cube: click an axis or a cube face to align the camera to that view instantly; click the home icon to reset the camera.
guide.start.viewport.dolly: Alt + right-drag: dolly in/out; mouse wheel: zoom.
guide.start.viewport.orbit: Alt + left-drag: orbit (rotate the view around the target).
guide.start.viewport.p1: The Scene panel is the 3D viewport for editing your scene. Camera control is Maya-style: everything starts with holding Alt.
guide.start.viewport.pan: Alt + middle-drag: pan (grab the world and drag it).
guide.start.viewport.pick: Left-click selects an entity; hold Ctrl or Shift to add/toggle selection; drag the left button on empty space for a marquee selection.
guide.start.viewport.tip1: Snap increments apply while Ctrl-dragging a gizmo; drag direction and wheel zoom direction can be inverted in Preferences.
guide.start.viewport.title: Viewport Navigation
guide.start.viewport.tools: The viewport toolbar offers translate/rotate/scale and pivot edit, local/world space, snap settings, 2D/3D toggle and frame-selected; the View dropdown holds render modes (wireframe/shaded/textured), the grid toggle, physics debug, show flags (gizmos, light/camera icons, colliders, skybox, bounding boxes, world axis, stats overlay, navmesh, streaming), plus reset camera and top/front/side views.
guide.start.viewport.warn1: The View/Perspective, View/Top etc. entries and the grid-toggle hotkey listed in the Hotkey Reference are not wired up yet — use the viewport toolbar or the context menu instead.
guide.world.bt.hk1: Enter Play to watch live node status
guide.world.bt.p1: Behavior trees use BehaviorTree.CPP XML assets. The Behavior Tree component on an entity specifies the tree file and the tick rate; in Play, the runtime loads the tree into a shared context and advances it at each agent's own cadence. The BT Visualizer panel shows the whole tree as an indented list with status dots.
guide.world.bt.s1: Add the Behavior Tree component to an entity and set the tree file under "Behavior Tree Asset (.xml)"; a "Tick Rate (Hz)" of 0 means once per gameplay frame.
guide.world.bt.s2: Agents that need perception can set "Sight Range", "Sight Cone Angle" and "Hearing Range" (0 = engine default); the runtime perception pass reads these every gameplay frame.
guide.world.bt.s3: Click "Open in BT Visualizer" in the Inspector, or open the panel from the Window menu; the panel follows the currently selected entity and shows its tree.
guide.world.bt.tip1: During Play, the dot in front of each node shows running/success/failure/skipped; the translucent "ghost" dot next to it records the most recent completed result with a transition counter - the cadence follows the component's tick rate, not the frame rate.
guide.world.bt.tip2: In edit mode the panel uses lenient loading for a structure-only preview: unregistered game actions are replaced with inert stub nodes, so a tree displaying fine does not mean its actions are implemented. The panel caches by (entity, path, file mtime), so saving the XML re-reads automatically; "Reload" forces a refresh.
guide.world.bt.title: Behavior Trees: AI Decisions and Visualization
guide.world.bt.warn1: If the tree path is empty or the XML fails to parse, the agent executes nothing at runtime; parse error details go to the Console.
guide.world.fx.p1: Particles come in two layers: the Particle Editor (merged into the Material Graph workbench as the "Particle Editor" tab) edits .particles.json emitter descriptions; the Particle Emitter component on an entity references that asset and the runtime emits from it.
guide.world.fx.s1: Tune the fields directly in the particle tab: max particles, emit rate, lifetime range, velocity range, gravity, start/end size and start/end color, world space; or start from a preset (Default/Smoke/Fire/Sparks/Snow/Magic) and click "Apply Preset".
guide.world.fx.s2: Use Play/Pause/Step/Reset and the "Speed" multiplier to watch the built-in 3D orbital preview: left-drag rotates, mouse wheel zooms; the fill bar at the top of the canvas shows alive count versus capacity.
guide.world.fx.s3: Enter a path in "File": "Save" writes the .particles.json, "Load" reads it back for further tuning, and "Defaults" resets everything.
guide.world.fx.s4: Add the Particle Emitter component to an entity and drag the .particles.json into "Particle Asset". Once an asset is set, the quick-tune fields on the component (emit rate / lifetime) are ignored at runtime - the asset drives the emitter.
guide.world.fx.s5: For large particle counts, check "GPU Simulation": every GPU-enabled emitter gets its own GPU particle pool simulated by compute shaders. Also confirm the "GPU Particles" feature is enabled in the render pipeline (the Render Pipeline tab of the Rendering workbench).
guide.world.fx.tip1: The 3D preview in the panel is a CPU "shadow simulation" that never touches engine particle state; the engine count and the preview count are displayed separately at the bottom for comparison.
guide.world.fx.title: Particles: CPU Simulation and GPU Particles
guide.world.fx.warn1: The GPU path requires compute shader support; if unsupported, the emitter automatically falls back to CPU simulation. GPU particles always simulate in world space with a procedural sprite - authored textures and local-space emission are CPU-only.
guide.world.nav.hk1: Enter Play to verify agents pathfind along the navmesh
guide.world.nav.p1: Baking is driven by Recast/Detour: the panel gathers CPU triangles from Mesh Renderers (transformed to world space) and ground quads at Terrain entities, voxelizes them into a single-tile navmesh and writes it to .navmesh.bin; bake settings are saved separately to .navmesh.json so the same bake can be reproduced later.
guide.world.nav.s1: In "Settings", tune cell size, cell height, agent radius, agent height, max slope and climb step to match your character.
guide.world.nav.s2: Set "Path" to the sidecar named after the current scene: for scenes/level.scene.json enter scenes/level.navmesh.json - Play mode and the overlay only look for "<scene name>.navmesh.bin" in that one location.
guide.world.nav.s3: Click "Bake". Baking runs on a background thread and the editor stays responsive; the "Bake Result" section and the Console report polygon, vertex and timing statistics. "Cancel" does not interrupt the computation but discards the result when it finishes.
guide.world.nav.s4: Check "Show Overlay" to inspect the wireframe (bright orange = boundary edges) - it is the same switch as the navmesh entry in the Scene view "Show Flags" menu, and the overlay refreshes automatically after a re-bake.
guide.world.nav.s5: Add the Nav Agent component to AI entities: set radius, height, max speed, max acceleration and arrive radius; the target can be a fixed "Target Position" or a "Target Entity", and check "Auto Repath" to chase moving targets.
guide.world.nav.tip1: If you get "no walkable geometry found", the scene lacks Mesh Renderers with loadable meshes or Terrain entities. The "Bounds Min/Max" fields are informational only nowadays - the actual bake extent is derived from the gathered geometry.
guide.world.nav.title: NavMesh: Baking and Nav Agents
guide.world.nav.warn1: The output file name is derived from "Path" by stripping the .navmesh.json suffix and appending .navmesh.bin; if it is not the sidecar named after the current scene, the runtime silently disables navigation. The navmesh is not re-baked automatically after scene geometry changes - remember to bake again.
guide.world.net.hk1: Enter Play so the session actually runs
guide.world.net.p1: Replication is declared with components: Network Object is the gatekeeper (net_id is assigned by the server at spawn and read-only in the panel; "Owner" is editable), and Net Transform syncs the pose with sync rate, interpolation window, tolerance and authority mode. Net Animator and Net Rigidbody are editable today but not yet simulated at runtime - the Inspector badges them honestly.
guide.world.net.s1: Add Net* components such as Net Transform to entities that must sync - the editor auto-attaches the Network Object gatekeeper. Without the gatekeeper, no Net* component on the entity will sync.
guide.world.net.s2: Open the network workbench. The stats tab shows session mode, client count and replication diagnostics (network object count, registered transforms, delta entries sent, interest radius), and plots per-peer 60-second rolling curves of RTT, in/out bandwidth and packet loss at one sample per second.
guide.world.net.s3: Switch to the "LAN Discovery" tab: "Refresh" scans for about 3 seconds and the table lists servers broadcasting on the LAN (name/address/ping/last seen); "Join" connects as a client, and the status line offers "Leave".
guide.world.net.tip1: A net_id of 0 means the entity has not been spawned by the server yet - a normal edit-time state that you neither need nor can fill in; the field meant for designers is "Owner".
guide.world.net.title: Networking: Components, Sessions and Diagnostics
guide.world.net.warn1: Sessions are pumped by the runtime's fixed step; the editor itself does not pump the network - a freshly joined session stays in connecting state until you enter Play. Only one session per process at a time; the editor's built-in entry point is "Join" (client) only - hosting or a dedicated server must be started by game code through the session API.
guide.world.stream.p1: World streaming splits a large world into scene fragments (chunks) that are loaded and unloaded asynchronously by camera distance. The streamer config and the chunk registry are scene-level data serialized with the scene JSON; every change made in the panel enters the undo history.
guide.world.stream.p2: No manual registration is needed when packaging: the bundle dependency scan recursively follows fragment scenes referenced by the main scene, plus the meshes, textures and even nested streaming chunk tables those fragments reference.
guide.world.stream.s1: Check "Enable Streaming" and pick a "Mode": radial (open world) or rectangular (top-down); then set the load radius and unload radius. The panel automatically keeps the unload radius at least as large as the load radius to avoid boundary thrashing.
guide.world.stream.s2: Scale "Memory Budget" (MiB), "Max Pending Loads" and "Per-frame Time Budget" (ms) to your project to bound how much work the streamer does each frame.
guide.world.stream.s3: Click "Add Chunk" in the "Chunks" table: a new chunk is centered on the current editor camera position. Edit center, radius and "Fragment Path" (a scene JSON fragment relative to the project root) per row; "Use Camera" re-centers any time. The limit is 256 chunks.
guide.world.stream.s4: Check "Preview in Scene View": the editor runs the real streamer and spawns chunk entities into the Hierarchy as the camera moves, and the table gains a "State" column (loaded/loading/unloading/unloaded).
guide.world.stream.s5: Open the streaming overlay in the Scene view "Show Flags" menu to visualize each chunk's radius ring plus the camera's load/unload radii.
guide.world.stream.tip1: The streamer config has no runtime setters: any settings change rebuilds the whole streamer (it rebuilds only after you release the slider, so scrubbing a radius does not stutter).
guide.world.stream.title: World Streaming: Chunked Large Worlds
guide.world.stream.warn1: Chunk entities spawned by the preview are temporary: before saving the scene the editor destroys the streamer and removes them, so streamed content is never baked into the main scene. Do not hand-edit or reference preview entities; the preview toggle itself is session state and is never saved.
guide.world.sys.hk1: Enter Play to populate the ECS systems list
guide.world.sys.p1: The Systems panel has two tabs: "Player Loop" lists engine-level registered callbacks grouped by 8 phases (initialization / early update / fixed update / update / late update / pre-render / post-render / end of frame), with an enable toggle, name, priority and last-frame time per row; "ECS Systems" lists the flecs systems of the active scene with group, last-frame ms and matched entity count.
guide.world.sys.s1: First set the refresh interval (0.1/0.5/1/5 s) and the filter text (case-insensitive substring match) at the top; both tabs share them.
guide.world.sys.s2: In "Player Loop", use the row checkbox to temporarily disable a callback and correlate against the "Last (ms)" column to localize performance or behavior problems.
guide.world.sys.s3: Switch to "ECS Systems": the list is stably sorted by group + name; unchecking a row disables that system immediately so you can observe the scene's behavior change.
guide.world.sys.title: Systems Panel: Player Loop and ECS
guide.world.sys.warn1: The enable toggles here are session-local runtime state and are never written to the scene or the project; ECS systems are recreated on every Play start, so changes do not carry over to the next run.
guide.world.terrain.p1: The Terrain panel edits the same resident terrain used by Scene View, picking, and physics. Height and splat data persist in a .terrain.json metadata file plus a sibling .terrain.bin binary; brush strokes update affected render chunks immediately and Save writes that resident asset to disk.
guide.world.terrain.p2: The "Info" section shows vertex counts, world size, chunk statistics, plus the sampled height and the four splat weights at the cursor; the "Preview" section renders an ASCII heightmap thumbnail for a quick sanity check of the overall relief.
guide.world.terrain.s1: Under "New Terrain Parameters", set vertex W/H, world size, max height and chunk size, then click "New" in the toolbar. Both dimensions should preferably satisfy (chunks x chunkSize) + 1.
guide.world.terrain.s2: In the "Brush" section pick a tool: Sculpt offers Raise/Lower/Smooth/Flatten modes, while Splat paints up the weight of the selected layer (0-3). Then tune radius and strength.
guide.world.terrain.s3: Check "Paint in Scene View (LMB drag)" to stroke directly in the Scene view by holding the left mouse button. The colored surface ring is the authoritative footprint; manual Cursor X/Z values are terrain-local coordinates.
guide.world.terrain.s4: Fill in the .terrain.json path in the toolbar "Path" field and click "Save". Saving also writes the .terrain.bin sidecar; no reload or duplicate terrain copy is created.
guide.world.terrain.s5: Select a scene entity, add the Terrain component, drag the .terrain.json into Terrain Path, then click Edit Terrain in the Inspector. The editor opens and focuses the Terrain panel and binds its resident terrain automatically.
guide.world.terrain.s6: For shaped strokes, load a grayscale brush mask and adjust rotation, hardness, spacing, scatter, and rotation jitter. Fast Scene-view drags are resampled into a continuous stroke, and Flatten locks its target height for the whole drag.
guide.world.terrain.s7: To paint ground materials, enable Splat Blend on the Terrain component, assign albedo/normal/mask textures to layers 0-3, select Splat in the Terrain panel, choose the target layer, and drag the blue brush ring over the surface.
guide.world.terrain.s8: To place or thin grass, flowers, and trees, add a Vegetation Scatter component, assign a model and area/density, enable Density Paint, then arm Paint in Scene. Drag the green ring to erase or restore density; terrain and foliage brushes are mutually exclusive.
guide.world.terrain.tip1: The panel keeps its own brush undo stack (up to 32 steps): press Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y while the panel is focused, or use the in-panel Undo/Redo buttons. One Scene-view drag records a single undo entry.
guide.world.terrain.title: Terrain: Sculpting and Layer Painting
guide.world.terrain.warn1: Terrain data does not live in the scene file, and the scene undo history does not cover brush edits. "New" and "Load" discard unsaved brush changes and clear the brush undo stack - always "Save" before leaving.
guide.world.tilemap.p1: The tile pipeline has three parts: the Sprite Editor produces a .sprites.json atlas description, the Tile Palette paints tile indices into a .tilemap.json grid, and the Tilemap component on an entity references both so the scene renderer can draw it in chunks.
guide.world.tilemap.p2: World mapping convention: 1 cell = 1 world unit in entity-local space (then multiplied by entity scale), rows grow in -Y, matching the palette's screen-space grid; "Cell Pixels" does not affect world size.
guide.world.tilemap.s1: First slice your atlas in the Sprite Editor; then link it in the Tile Palette's left column under "Sprites Asset (.sprites.json)", click "Refresh Palette" to load the numbered tile slots, and pick a brush (brush 0 is the eraser).
guide.world.tilemap.s2: Set "Map Size" W/H (max 1024 per dimension) and "Cell Pixels" (display size inside the panel only). On the right grid: left-click paints, right-click erases, middle-drag pans; "Fill All / Clear All" handle bulk operations.
guide.world.tilemap.s3: Enter a path under "Persistence (.tilemap.json)" and click "Save"; saving makes the Scene view reload this tilemap immediately, so edits are WYSIWYG.
guide.world.tilemap.s4: Add the Tilemap component to an entity and assign the .tilemap.json plus the sprite atlas. You can tune "Sort Order" (2D draw order), "Orientation" (orthogonal/isometric), color and visibility; the "Edit in Tile Palette" button opens the palette with the paths pre-filled.
guide.world.tilemap.s5: For collision, add the Tilemap Collider 2D component: on entering Play, all non-zero tile cells are greedily merged into boxes and attached to the entity as one static Box2D body; friction, bounciness, offset and trigger are all adjustable.
guide.world.tilemap.tip1: Cell 0 (empty) is neither rendered nor collidable; any non-zero tile id counts as solid.
guide.world.tilemap.title: Tilemap: Painting and 2D Collision
guide.world.tilemap.warn1: The tilemap collider is always static - even if a dynamic 2D rigidbody coexists on the entity, the tilemap body will not move with it (the Console warns about this).
